You said:
How can I keep Google Tasks and Apple Reminders synchronized on iPhone? Compare a shared task view, true two-way syncing and automation. Explain fields or behaviours that may not transfer and cite official sources.
ChatGPT said:
Google Tasks ↔ Apple Reminders on iPhone

Google Tasks and Apple Reminders don't have a built-in, native two-way sync. You can use both on your iPhone, but keeping their contents synchronized requires either a shared task interface, a third-party synchronization service, or automation.

The important distinction is whether you want to see all your tasks together or keep identical, editable copies in both systems.

1. Compare your three options

Approach

	

How it works

My recommendation: Start with a shared view if your main concern is missing tasks. Choose two-way synchronization only if you genuinely need to edit the same task from both Google Tasks and Apple Reminders.

A shared view is simpler because it avoids duplicate tasks, synchronization conflicts, and mismatched completion states.

2. Shared task view: simplest option

Use both apps, but avoid duplicating tasks.

Keep Google Tasks as the home for Google-related tasks and Apple Reminders for Siri, location-based alerts, and Apple-specific features.

You can use Google Calendar on iPhone to see and edit dated Google Tasks. However, this doesn't automatically include Apple Reminders. 
Google Tasks Help
+1

Apple Reminders supports multiple accounts, including iCloud, Exchange, and compatible CalDAV accounts. But adding your Google account to your iPhone does not establish Google Tasks synchronization. 
Apple Support (IE)
+1

To set up a practical shared workflow:

Enable iCloud Reminders under Settings → your name → iCloud → See All → Reminders.

Install Google Tasks and sign in.

Use Google Calendar to review dated Google Tasks.

For a single consolidated list, choose a third-party task app that explicitly supports both Google Tasks and Apple Reminders as live data sources.

Check whether a third-party app merely imports tasks or actually writes changes back to both services. A combined display alone isn't synchronization.

3. True two-way syncing: what to require
A true sync engine must track changes in both directions.

A real two-way service needs to support more than copying newly created tasks. It should:

Propagate title, notes, and date changes in both directions.

Mark matching tasks completed or reopened.

Handle deletion without recreating deleted tasks.

Preserve a stable mapping between Google and Apple task IDs.

Resolve simultaneous edits and prevent synchronization loops.

Google provides an official Tasks API for reading and updating tasks, but that API alone doesn't provide access to Apple Reminders. A third-party solution needs a separate supported mechanism for the Apple side. 
Google for Developers
+1

Important: I wouldn't treat any particular third-party service as verified full two-way sync without testing these behaviors. Some services advertise integration while only supporting one-way creation or limited fields.

4. Automation: most flexible, but more maintenance

Apple Shortcuts can automate Reminders-related workflows. Google's Tasks API supports task operations that can be used by a separate integration. 
Apple Support
+1

A practical setup is:

Step 1 — Read Apple Reminders

Create a shortcut that finds reminders in a dedicated list such as “Sync to Google.”

Step 2 — Schedule the workflow

Use a time-of-day automation or run it manually. A scheduled scan is more dependable than assuming every reminder edit triggers a shortcut.

Step 3 — Update Google Tasks

Send new or modified items to an integration using the Google Tasks API. Store task IDs to avoid duplicates.

Step 4 — Add reverse synchronization if needed

A separate process reads Google Tasks and updates matching Apple Reminders. Include conflict handling and deletion safeguards.

Shortcuts does not itself provide a ready-made Google Tasks ↔ Apple Reminders sync. A reverse workflow generally needs additional integration software or custom code, and iOS background execution can limit reliability.

5. Fields and behaviors that may not transfer

This is where most synchronization solutions become imperfect.

Field or behavior

	

Compatibility concern

No direct equivalent for every Apple priority or flag

Apple Reminders location triggers generally cannot be reproduced in Google Tasks




Attachments

	

May be dropped or replaced with links




Shared lists and assignments

	

Permissions and assignments may not survive




Deletions

	

Risk of accidental recreation or removal if sync rules are incomplete

These are potential compatibility issues, not a claim that every integration loses every field.

Two particularly important differences:

Dates and times: Google's Tasks API documents a due field that retains the date but discards the time portion when written through that field. Google's consumer apps can support scheduled task times, but the API does not expose all that scheduling information. This makes precise time-based synchronization difficult. 
Google for Developers
+1

Apple-specific features: Apple Reminders supports location-based alerts, attachments, and subtasks. Apple also warns that some Reminders features aren't available even when using supported non-iCloud accounts. 
Apple Support
+1

6. Which setup should you choose?

What matters most to you?

See all my tasks in one place
Edit tasks in either app and keep both updated
Automate selected tasks with custom rules

Keep both services separate and use a combined viewer where supported. This avoids duplicate data and sync conflicts.

Bottom line: For reliability, choose one app as the primary source of truth. A shared view is the lowest-maintenance option; full two-way sync is the most demanding; and automation is best when you want control over exactly which tasks move between systems.
